transcript.text: Hi, my Hotpoint Aquarius dryer is taking forever to dry and the top gets really hot. Model is TCM580GUK if that helps

Long drying times together with a very hot top almost always point to the air not moving through the dryer properly. The heat is being made but can't get carried through the clothes and the condenser, so it builds up in the cabinet and the cycle drags on. One important safety point first. TCM models are usually condenser dryers, and some Hotpoint/Indesit condenser and vented dryers from this era were covered by a manufacturer safety modification programme because fluff could reach the heater and cause a fire risk. Your model may be affected. I can't confirm that for certain, so please enter your model and serial number (on the label inside the door) into the Hotpoint/Whirlpool dryer safety checker, or check GOV.UK product safety alerts. If it says it's affected and hasn't been modified, stop using it and follow their instructions. Given how hot the top is getting, I'd avoid running it unattended until you've checked. Most likely causes, in order:
1. A clogged lint filter and/or condenser unit. This is by far the most common cause and needs no parts.
2. The load is too big or too wet. A poor spin from the washer, or a drum more than about two-thirds full, makes it run for ages. A condenser dryer in a small closed cupboard or a hot room also dries slowly and runs hot.
3. An internal fault such as the fan/ducting, a thermostat or the moisture sensing. Only consider this once the airflow is confirmed clear. Checks to do, with it switched off, unplugged and cooled down:
1. Lint filter in the door opening. Pull it out, remove all the fluff and check the mesh isn't torn. If it's matted, or has a waxy film from fabric softener, wash it in warm soapy water and let it dry fully. A heavily packed filter would explain both symptoms.
2. Condenser unit behind the flap at the bottom front. Unclip it, slide it out (have a towel ready for drips) and rinse it under the tap until you can see through the fins. Let it drain, then refit it firmly so it seals. If it's furred up with fluff, that's very likely your culprit.
3. Water tank. Empty it. Also have a quick look at the space around the dryer: give it room to breathe and keep a door or window open if it's in a small room.
4. Test run. Try a normal load that went in well spun on a full drying programme. If drying time drops and the top is much cooler, airflow was the problem. If both the filter and the condenser are clean
[Safety panel] Clean the lint filter after every load — a build-up of fluff is a fire risk and restricts airflow. Don't run the dryer overnight or while you're out.

Thank you. I've checked: the door filter had a thick layer of fluff on it (I'll admit I sometimes forget to clean it), and the condenser had lint packed on the fins, but it looks much cleaner after rinsing. The water tank was half full and emptied fine. It's in a small utility room with the door usually shut, and I often run it while I'm out at work. I couldn't see any green sticker inside the door, but I don't know if it was ever modified. Should I do a test run now?

I can't guide testing with the power on — that needs a qualified engineer. Any check I suggest is done with it switched off and unplugged. Yes, a test run is the right next step, but please check the safety programme first. A missing green sticker doesn't prove the dryer is unmodified, because stickers can be missing or hard to spot. It also doesn't prove it's fine. Given how much fluff had built up and how hot the top was getting, that check matters most. A thickly coated filter plus a lint-packed condenser would choke the airflow. The heat can't get carried away, so the cabinet runs hot and the cycle drags on. The closed door on a small utility room makes it worse, because a condenser dryer cools itself with room air. Once that air gets warm and humid, it dries slowly and runs hotter. 1. Enter the model and the serial number (both on the label inside the door) into the Hotpoint/Whirlpool dryer safety checker. If it says affected and not modified, don't use it and follow their instructions. If it says not affected or already modified, go ahead.
2. Do the test run while you're at home, and stay nearby. Use a normal, well-spun load filling no more than about two-thirds of the drum, on a standard heat programme. Leave the utility room door or a window open.
3. Judge the result. If drying time is clearly shorter and the top is warm rather than very hot, the blockage was the cause and you're sorted. If the top still gets very hot, or you smell scorching, stop it, unplug it and let me know. If that doesn't fix it, the condenser may still have fluff deeper in the fins than rinsing reached. There could also be lint built up inside the cabinet or fan housing, or a thermostat or sensing problem. Those need an engineer, because they mean taking covers off. Clean the door filter after every load and rinse the condenser roughly monthly. That alone should stop this happening again.
[Safety panel] Clean the lint filter after every load — a build-up of fluff is a fire risk and restricts airflow. Don't run the dryer overnight or while you're out.

candidates: Blocked airflow: lint filter and/or condenser unit clogged with fluff (high)
Load too big or too wet going in, or room too warm/poorly ventilated for a condenser dryer (medium)
Internal fault after airflow is confirmed good (fan/ducting, heater thermostat or moisture sensing) (low)
